children.text: The objection to building a portfolio office is almost always the same: we cannot afford it. Chapter 15 answers it directly with a cost-benefit table, and then makes a harder point: the table omits the most important number, the cost of failure. This lesson works through the book's business case, explains how to frame the cost of failure honestly, and gives you a structure for making the same case in your own organization.

A business case for management infrastructure is unusual because its benefits are mostly avoided losses. Nothing new appears when a portfolio office works; things simply stop going wrong. That makes the case easy to dismiss and important to make carefully.
The aim is a case that a budget office, a board or a legislature can test: costs that are explicit, benefits tied to specific risks, and a clear statement of what is assumed.
What the Portfolio Office Costs

Figure 15.9 of the book costs a staffed portfolio office for Vermont at about $0.85 million to $1.3 million a year, or roughly $4 million to $6.4 million over four to five years. The largest line is the five pillar program managers, shared across agencies and hospitals, at $500,000 to $850,000 a year. The senior Portfolio Manager, with the PfMP credential, is costed at $180,000 to $220,000 a year; two analysts at $120,000 to $160,000; and portfolio-management software at $50,000 to $100,000.

Each line is paired with the benefit it buys. The Portfolio Manager provides single accountability for the January 2028 deadline and directly avoids R-10, the risk that the transformation is managed as a collection of projects. The analysts maintain the master schedule, the risk register and the dashboard. The software provides real-time visibility, resource optimization and an audit trail for Act 68. The program managers carry delivery accountability and critical-path management within each pillar.

The book's comparison is with the money the office coordinates. At under 1% a year of the $195 million first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award alone, before counting any savings from reference-based pricing, the office is a small fraction of the investment it protects.

children.text: The Cost of Failure

The book's central argument is that the cost-benefit table leaves out the cost of failure. Without adequate portfolio infrastructure, Vermont risks delivering the January 2028 Strategic Plan as a descriptive document rather than a binding commitment, which the book's chapter on political sustainability identifies as the most dangerous failure mode. That outcome is not free. In the book's words, it is a multi-billion-dollar one: the continuation of the deficit trajectory Oliver Wyman projected, the failure of thirteen of fourteen hospitals to reach sustainability, and the loss of the political window that the mandatory architecture has opened.

Cross-industry evidence points the same way at smaller scale. PMI's 2017 Pulse of the Profession put the waste from poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending. That is an average across industries and organizations, not a forecast for any Vermont program, so it should not be multiplied into a precise saving. Its use in a business case is to establish order of magnitude: typical waste from poor delivery is several times larger, as a share of spending, than the cost of the office proposed here.

There is also federal money at stake. The book notes in answering the third objection that Rural Health Transformation Program funds are contingent on demonstrated progress, so a portfolio that misses its components risks clawback. The office's cost, it argues, is less than 2% of a single year of the value it protects.

body.message: A business case for management infrastructure is most credible when it is conservative. State costs as ranges, tie benefits to named risks, use cross-industry figures for scale only, and say plainly which benefits are avoided losses rather than new savings.
body.title: Do not overclaim savings

children.text: Framing Avoided Losses

Because most of a portfolio office's value is avoided loss, the strongest framing ties each cost line to the specific risks it reduces. The risk register from Track 4 supplies this. The Portfolio Manager is costed against R-10 and, through the portfolio office, R-03. The Technology program manager is costed against R-01 and R-06, the two Technology risks that propagate into Economics and Clinical. The Economics program manager is costed against R-08, the risk that safety-net hospitals are penalized because social-risk adjustment arrives too late.

Linking costs to risks lets a decision-maker ask the right question. Not whether the office is affordable in the abstract, but whether paying for a given role is worth the reduction in a specific, scored risk. A $200,000 role that materially reduces a risk scored 20 on a portfolio worth hundreds of millions is an easy decision once the link is drawn.

The same logic answers the question of timing. A portfolio office hired after the critical gating decisions are made can only report on their consequences. Its value is highest before the gates it protects, which is why the book's roadmap puts the Portfolio Manager in seat by January 2027, nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect.

children.text: Making the Case in a Hospital or Health System

The structure transfers directly to a hospital or health system. Inventory the transformation components and their combined budget. Build the risk register and identify the cross-component risks no single program owns. Cost the portfolio function at the scale your organization needs, which may be one portfolio lead and shared program leads rather than a full office. Then present the cost as a share of the investment it coordinates and tie each role to the risks it reduces.

Hospitals have one advantage in making the case: their financial exposure to transformation is direct and visible. Under a global budget, a hospital whose payment and clinical redesign are out of sequence feels the result in its operating margin, often within a year. Linking the portfolio function to protecting that margin is usually more persuasive to a board than any general argument about governance.

Whatever the setting, include the cost of doing nothing. A business case that only lists the cost of the office invites the answer 'not this year'. One that also states, with appropriate caution, what the organization stands to lose without it, invites a real decision.

children.text: Testing the Case Before You Present It

Before presenting, test the case the way a skeptical budget office would. Are the costs complete, including software, training and the time of people seconded to the office? Are the risks it claims to reduce on a real register with real scores? Are cross-industry figures used for scale only? Is the comparison base, the investment coordinated, stated accurately and current?

Then test it against the objections in the next lesson. The most common, that existing governance already covers this, is best answered inside the business case itself, by showing what the governance body cannot do without a portfolio office to supply it with data.

A case that survives these tests is short. It fits on one page: the investment coordinated, the cost of the office as a share of it, the three or four top risks it reduces, and the date by which it must exist to be useful.

The one-page version: the portfolio office costs under 1% a year of what it coordinates, directly reduces the portfolio's highest-scored risks, and is worth most if it exists before the gates it protects.
